name: arm9-abm-meanfield
title: Arm 9 — Agent-based model vs its mean-field SBML reduction (the adversarial arm)
question: The whole investigation assumes the model you start with is an SBML/ODE network. But can an AGENT-BASED model — a population of discrete individuals with stochastic interactions — even BE an SBML/Tellurium model? If you reduce it to a mean-field ODE and run it in libroadrunner/CVODE, where does that reduction hold and where does it structurally break?
hypothesis: A well-mixed stochastic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey ABM (integer counts, Gillespie-SSA birth/predation/death events) reduces to the deterministic Lotka-Volterra ODE — a valid SBML/Tellurium model — ONLY in the large-population limit (Kurtz/van Kampen): as the system size K grows the SSA ensemble mean converges to the ODE, but at small K demographic stochasticity, discreteness and EXTINCTION (an absorbing state the neutrally-stable ODE orbits can never reach) dominate and the ODE misses the dynamics entirely. The ODE can represent neither the variance nor the extinction probability at any K.
objective: Build the ABM as a genuine model (native Gillespie-SSA process over integer populations), build its mean-field ODE reduction as real Antimony integrated by libroadrunner/CVODE, and QUANTIFY the divergence at a large vs a small population scale — relative error of the SSA ensemble mean against the ODE, and the fraction of SSA runs that go extinct (which the ODE can never show) — to answer "can it even be SBML?" honestly, with numbers.
description: The adversarial / ablation arm of the SBML-decomposition investigation: the case built to BREAK the naive "any model is an SBML model" claim that arms 1-8 implicitly rest on. The SAME Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system is realised two ways. (1) THE ABM — a well-mixed population of DISCRETE individuals (integer prey/predator counts) whose prey birth (propensity r*X), predation (a/K*X*Y), predator birth (b/K*X*Y) and predator death (m*Y) are STOCHASTIC EVENTS, advanced by the exact Gillespie SSA (direct method) in a native process-bigraph PredatorPreyABMProcess. There is no continuous RHS for CVODE; one run is one stochastic realisation, so an ensemble is needed for statistics. This model is NOT an SBML model. (2) THE MEAN-FIELD REDUCTION — the deterministic Lotka-Volterra ODE (dx/dt = r*x - a*x*y, dy/dt = b*x*y - m*y) as Antimony integrated by libroadrunner/CVODE in a TelluriumProcess, carried on the predator_prey_meanfield generator's config.model so the Model page shows exactly what the SBML reduction is. The 1/K system-size factor on the quadratic propensities makes the density X/K obey the same scale-free ODE at every K, so K is a clean knob from "stochastic handful of individuals" (K=8) to "effectively continuous" (K=400). abm_ensemble measures, per scale, the SSA ensemble mean/variance + extinction fraction; the finding compares the mean (in density units) to the ODE. Nothing is tuned to make the ABM match the ODE — the small-K divergence is the point.
claim: An agent-based model reduces to an SBML/Tellurium mean-field ODE ONLY in the large-population, well-mixed, deterministic limit; it structurally cannot capture stochasticity, discreteness, extinction, or individual heterogeneity. MEASURED (Lotka-Volterra, base rates r=a=b=m=1, start density (1.8, 1.0), horizon ~2 periods): at a LARGE population scale K=400 (80 SSA runs) the mean-field ODE reproduces the SSA ensemble mean to a max relative error of 4.9% with 0% of runs going extinct — the reduction is VALID. At a SMALL scale K=8 (200 SSA runs) the ensemble mean diverges from the ODE by 68% max relative error and 94% of runs go EXTINCT before the horizon, hitting an absorbing state (prey or predator count 0) that the neutrally-stable ODE — which simply orbits forever — can never reach. The ODE additionally cannot represent the ensemble variance at ANY K. So "can an ABM be an SBML model?" has an honest, quantified answer: yes, but only as its large-population mean-field limit, and that reduction silently discards exactly the stochastic/discrete phenomena (extinction, demographic noise) that are often the biological point. This breaks the naive "just write it as SBML" claim.

expected_behavior.name: arm9-meanfield-valid-only-at-large-N
expected_behavior.observable: relative error of the Gillespie-SSA ABM ensemble mean against the mean-field Lotka-Volterra ODE (libroadrunner/CVODE), and the fraction of SSA runs that go extinct, at a large (K=400) vs a small (K=8) population scale
expected_behavior.condition: at the LARGE scale the ODE matches the SSA ensemble mean within tolerance (max relative error < 0.12; measured 0.049) with no extinction (extinct_fraction == 0), AND at the SMALL scale the reduction demonstrably breaks — a non-trivial fraction of runs go extinct (extinct_fraction > 0.2; measured 0.94) while the ODE persists (never extinct), and the ensemble mean diverges markedly from the ODE (max relative error substantially larger than at the large scale).
expected_behavior.rationale: The Kurtz/van Kampen large-population limit guarantees the SSA ensemble mean converges to the mean-field ODE as the system size grows, so a faithful ABM + a correct ODE reduction MUST agree at large K; the stochastic Lotka-Volterra system is not persistent (it reaches an absorbing extinction state with probability 1 at finite size), so a small-K ensemble MUST show extinction the deterministic ODE cannot. The behavior therefore gates the exact adversarial claim: reduction valid at large N, structurally invalid (extinction + divergence) at small N.

findings.summary: REDUCTION VALID AT LARGE N — at population scale K=400 (80 Gillespie-SSA runs, ~2 Lotka-Volterra periods) the mean-field ODE integrated by libroadrunner/CVODE reproduces the SSA ensemble mean to a max relative error of 4.9% (mean 1.0%), and 0% of runs go extinct. This is the Kurtz large-population limit in action: at enough individuals the discrete stochastic model and its continuous deterministic SBML reduction agree, so the ABM genuinely DOES reduce to an SBML model here.

REDUCTION INVALID AT SMALL N — at scale K=8 (200 SSA runs) 94% of runs go EXTINCT before the horizon (prey or predator count hits 0, an absorbing state), while the mean-field ODE — neutrally stable closed orbits — simply cycles forever and NEVER goes extinct. The SSA ensemble mean diverges from the ODE by 68% max relative error. The deterministic SBML reduction misses the single most important qualitative behaviour of the small-population system (that it dies out).

STRUCTURAL LIMIT, NOT A TOLERANCE — the gap is not something a finer integrator or looser tolerance closes. The ODE state is (prey, predator) concentrations; it has no representation of integer discreteness, of demographic noise variance, or of the extinction probability, at ANY K. Those are properties of the ensemble and the absorbing boundary, which a single deterministic trajectory cannot carry. The ABM was NOT tuned to match the ODE — the large-N agreement and the small-N divergence are both measured.

FEASIBILITY STATEMENT — "can an ABM even be an SBML/Tellurium model?" Answer: yes, but ONLY as its large-population, well-mixed, deterministic mean-field limit. That reduction is a real, runnable SBML model (the predator_prey_meanfield composite's Antimony) and is faithful when individuals are many; it silently discards stochasticity, discreteness, extinction and individual heterogeneity, which at small population size ARE the behaviour. This is the adversarial result that breaks the naive "just decompose/rewrite any model as SBML" claim the rest of the investigation operates under.

arm9-meanfield-valid-only-at-large-N.detail: LARGE K=400 (80 SSA runs): ODE matches SSA ensemble mean to max rel err 0.049, extinct_fraction 0.00 — reduction VALID. SMALL K=8 (200 SSA runs): extinct_fraction 0.94 (ODE never extinct), max rel err 0.685 — reduction INVALID. Measured, real Gillespie SSA + real libroadrunner/CVODE ODE; ABM not tuned to the ODE.

verdict: Passing — the adversarial claim is confirmed with numbers: the ABM reduces to its mean-field SBML/Tellurium ODE (4.9% max rel err, 0% extinction) only at large population (K=400), and the reduction structurally breaks at small population (K=8: 94% extinction the ODE can never show, 68% max rel err). An ABM CAN be an SBML model, but only as its large-population deterministic limit, which discards the stochasticity/discreteness/extinction that is often the point.
caveats: The mean-field ODE IS a faithful SBML reduction at large population — the arm is not an argument against SBML, but a quantification of the limit (large N, well-mixed, deterministic) in which the reduction is valid.

The specific extinction fractions (0% at K=400, 94% at K=8) are for this Lotka-Volterra parameterisation and horizon (~2 periods); the qualitative result (valid at large N, extinction-dominated at small N) is the Kurtz/van-Kampen limit and is parameterisation-independent, but the exact crossover scale is model-specific.
The ABM here is WELL-MIXED (no spatial grid); spatial/heterogeneous ABMs are even further from an ODE reduction, so this is the FAVOURABLE case for SBML and still breaks at small N.
